title: CEO Interview with Dr. Stefan Pastine of Thintronics - Semiwiki
gist: Thintronics CEO Stefan Pastine argues that package dielectric materials (build-up films in substrates) are becoming the binding constraint on AI/HPC performance as SerDes rates move from 224G to 448G, and that the industry's near-total reliance on a single unnamed Japanese supplier is a COVID-style single point of failure. The $20M Series A startup, negotiating a $50M CHIPS Act award, pitches ultra-low-loss dielectrics plus vertical integration (molecule-to-substrate) and a roadmap toward one unified dielectric across PCB, substrate and interposer; the piece is promotional and gives no performance numbers, customers or volumes.

insights.claim: As interconnect data rates move from 224G toward 448G, the dielectric materials inside chip substrates, not the silicon itself, are becoming the limiting factor for signal loss, power consumption and heat in advanced packages.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: The 448G transition is a catalyst for substrate/materials suppliers; low-loss dielectrics become a gating input for next-gen AI networking and accelerators.
insights.quote: the dielectric materials inside every chip substrate (managing heat, signal loss, and power) are running into real limits

insights.claim: Semiconductor performance can no longer be driven by silicon alone; the materials surrounding and connecting the chip increasingly determine what the chip can actually deliver.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Supports a value-shift thesis toward packaging, substrates and interconnect materials as the next locus of performance gains and margin capture.
insights.quote: semiconductor performance can no longer be driven by silicon alone

insights.claim: Incumbent package dielectric materials were engineered for a much slower performance era and cannot hit the performance targets that customers' next-generation packages are being designed around, with no easy drop-in substitute available.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Roadmap risk for chip/package designers implies qualification windows opening for alternative dielectric suppliers during the 448G design cycle.
insights.quote: their next-generation packages are designed around performance targets that the incumbent material can't hit, and there's no easy substitute sitting on the shelf
insights.locator: What keeps your customers up at night?

insights.claim: AI accelerators and the networking tying them together hit the dielectric performance ceiling first because they push data rates harder and faster than any other segment, making hyperscale AI packaging, high-speed networking and next-gen ASICs the most urgent demand for low-loss dielectrics.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: AI networking/custom ASIC buildouts are the lead indicator for adoption of new substrate materials; watch 448G switch and ASIC package announcements.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: The same dielectric-loss physics problem extends beyond AI into high-performance computing and advanced RF/mmWave systems, giving low-loss package dielectrics a multi-market addressable opportunity.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Suggests optionality beyond the AI cycle for low-loss dielectric suppliers, though AI is the near-term driver.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: Virtually the entire semiconductor industry sources its substrate dielectric (build-up film) material from a single supplier based in Japan, creating a single point of failure at the center of the semiconductor supply chain.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Concentrated supply of a critical packaging input is a pricing-power and disruption risk for AI hardware; the incumbent (unnamed in the article) holds a chokepoint position worth tracking.
insights.quote: virtually the entire industry sources this material from a single supplier, based in Japan

insights.claim: The single-source dependence on package dielectrics mirrors the single-point-of-failure dynamic that shut down auto plants during COVID, except it now sits at the center rather than the edge of the semiconductor supply chain.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Frames an underappreciated tail risk to AI hardware output; any geopolitical or logistical disruption to the supplier could halt package production broadly.
insights.quote: That's the exact same single-point-of-failure dynamic that shut down auto plants during COVID, except this time it sits at the center of the semiconductor supply chain

insights.claim: Customers face a simultaneous mandate to hit higher performance targets and de-risk their supply chain, and the same incumbent dielectric material is failing them on both fronts, so solving physics without solving supply risk does not solve the problem.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Dual pain point (performance plus second-sourcing) raises the odds that OEMs actively qualify a domestic alternative supplier.
insights.quote: Solving the physics without solving the supply chain risk doesn't really solve the problem.

insights.claim: Thintronics, founded in 2019 and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, closed a $20 million Series A in 2024 and is negotiating a $50 million CHIPS Act award, signalling US policy interest in onshoring package dielectric supply.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A pending CHIPS award would indicate government prioritization of packaging-materials sovereignty; watch for finalization as a validation milestone.

insights.claim: US domestic materials majors 3M, Rogers and Isola are developing their own build-up film alternatives, which Thintronics' CEO reads as confirmation that the package dielectric bottleneck is real.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Multiple credible entrants targeting the incumbent's build-up film position; watch 3M and Rogers for packaging-materials announcements and share gains.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like

insights.claim: Thintronics claims its differentiation is vertical integration: a team spanning molecular-level chemists, mechanical engineers for thermal/mechanical stress, and electrical engineers who have shipped substrates into production, whereas incumbents and domestic majors optimize only one layer of the stack.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: The moat claim rests on team/integration rather than disclosed material specs; no performance data is given, so treat it as unproven until qualification wins are announced.
insights.quote: We're built to optimize the whole path from molecule to shipped product.
insights.locator: Where Thintronics differentiates is vertical integration

insights.claim: Building a better dielectric film in isolation is not the hard part of the package bottleneck; the difficulty lies in solving material, process and system-level performance together.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Implies that material-only suppliers may struggle with adoption; integration and process support could decide winners among challengers.
insights.quote: building a better film in isolation isn't the hard part of this problem
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like

insights.claim: Stefan Pastine previously founded Connora Technologies (Recyclamine recyclable epoxy thermoset), which Aditya Birla Chemicals acquired in 2019 and applied to recyclable wind turbine blades.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Founder has a prior exit commercializing a polymer platform with a major chemicals acquirer, a relevant precedent for eventual strategic exit.
insights.locator: Stefan Pastine PhD is an American chemist

insights.claim: Dielectric materials within a single package today are a patchwork across PCB, substrate and interposer layers, often from different suppliers, and every material interface leaks performance and adds reliability risk.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Identifies a hidden cost in heterogeneous packaging that a single-platform supplier could monetize.
insights.quote: every interface between those materials is a place where performance leaks out and reliability risk creeps in
insights.locator: What new features/technology are you working on?

insights.claim: Thintronics is developing a unified dielectric system built on one material platform spanning PCB, substrate and interposer, so all layers of a package share consistent electrical and mechanical properties.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: If realized, a cross-layer platform would expand Thintronics' content per package well beyond build-up film; no timeline is given, so treat as long-dated roadmap.
insights.locator: Our roadmap is to fix that

insights.claim: With fabless design teams, Thintronics engages packaging and signal-integrity engineers first to show channel improvements, then escalates to architecture teams for system-level gains, before building with a qualified fab and moving to assembly.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Design-in path runs through signal-integrity wins; adoption will be slow and qualification-gated, typical of materials sales cycles.

insights.claim: For substrate factories, Thintronics focuses on process integration and economics, often embedding a field applications engineer with fab knowledge at the customer site, and for OSATs it supplies reference designs that help anchor volume at the fab.
insights.speaker: Stefan Pastine
insights.so_what: Heavy per-customer engineering support suggests high cost of adoption and a services-intensive early revenue model; volume depends on fab qualification.
insights.locator: With factories, the relationship runs differently
